extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science; readers studying Bacon's Novum Organum and method of induction
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes Francis Bacon's methodological criteria for interpreting Nature (the discovery of 'forms', use of induction, and practical precepts for producing natural effects). Targets how to investigate causes, construct operative precepts, and relate contemplation to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of the Form (forma / vera differentia / natura naturans)
rubrics_metrics.description: The central aim of human science is to find the 'Form' — the 'vera differentia' or 'natura naturans' (the inmost constitution or source of emanation) — which, when known, allows one to superinduce or generate a given nature on a body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon insists that discovery of the true form yields both contemplative truth and operative power: 'ex formarum inventione sequitur contemplatio vera, et operatic libera.' Forms should be sought by investigation (not by Platonic abstraction) and understood as the law or cause producing the given nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer proximate/material/efficient causes over remote/final causes
rubrics_metrics.description: In practical natural science the material and efficient (proximate) causes and the 'latens processus' and 'latens schematismus' are the proper objects of inquiry; remote and final causes are superficial and often corruptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon criticizes overreliance on final causes in physics ('causa finalis tantum abest ut prosit, ut etiam scientias corrumpat') and urges knowledge of inmost structure and secret processes rather than speculative remote causes assigned to theology or metaphysics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowing causes is necessary for true knowledge and power
rubrics_metrics.description: One cannot truly know a thing unless one knows its antecedents and conditions: knowledge of causes underpins both understanding and operative ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The maxim recurs: 'Recte ponitur; Vete sciu^ esse per causisque scire.' Practical power derives from causal knowledge; without it science remains 'imperfecta'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality of forms (applicability across dissimilar materials)
rubrics_metrics.description: A true knowledge of a Form enables producing the corresponding nature in materially dissimilar substrates; by contrast, knowledge only of efficient or material causes tends to be limited to certain similar subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon contrasts the artisan's empirical skill (limited to certain materials) with the scientist who knows forms and thus 'complectitur in materiis dissimillimis' and can bring about effects 'quae adhuc facta non sunt.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive method via Tables and Vindemiatio Prima; use 'permissio intellectus'
rubrics_metrics.description: The method begins with constructing Tables (to eliminate false explanations) and proceeds to a 'Vindemiatio Prima' (initial interpretation) in which imagination is allowed ('permissio intellectus') to frame hypotheses, subsequently to be rigorously tested by reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon's Book II outlines drawing up 'Tabulae' and using imaginative hypotheses as provisional steps; these hypotheses must then be subjected to logical scrutiny. He also enumerates 'auxilia' of induction (e.g., Praerogativae Instantiarum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin sciences from foundations nearest to action (active/fundamental foundations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the habit of abstract theorizing, it is safer to start and invigorate sciences from foundations that are ordered toward the active/operative part, so that the contemplative part is defined and determined by the active.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon recommends formulating directions 'simplici et minime abstruse' for generating a nature on a given body (e.g., making silver exhibit the yellow color of gold), thereby privileging practical, action-directed foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational precepts should be certain, liberal, and proximate to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A true operative precept must (1) not fail in practice, (2) not tie the operator to particular media or modes beyond his power to procure, and (3) be nearer to practice (less difficult) so it is accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon states the desirable character of an operative precept: 'ut sit certum, liberum, et disponens sive in ordine ad actionem.' Examples: precepts for inducing auric color in silver should not be experimentally deceptive nor overly constrained to specific media the operator cannot obtain.

rubrics_metrics.name: A true Form is necessary and (practically) sufficient for the given nature ('infallibiliter')
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon defines a true form as such that, when present, the given nature follows infallibly (with allowance for counteracting circumstances), and when absent the nature is absent; the form is found in the given nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He qualifies this by noting Mill-like objections: plurality of causes can mean the same effect may arise from different causes; thus 'infallibiliter' must be tempered by possible counteracting circumstances and multiple causal paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Couple imagination with reason but submit hypotheses to the rules of logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Although invention depends on the imagination and cannot be fully reduced to rules, cultivating logical habits and applying rules (conscious/artificial logic) can direct imagination into proper channels and subject its products to reasoned testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon acknowledges no complete 'Art of Invention' but insists on training mind with 'logical habits' so imaginative hypotheses are later verified by reason; 'Natural Logic' operates unconsciously, artificial logic makes it explicit and firmer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid abstract-only theorizing; make doctrines serve both knowledge and operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms and axioms should be useful both in knowing and in operating; what is most useful in practice should be true in science — active and contemplative pronouncements are the same when rightly constructed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon urges that doctrines be ordered 'ad partem activam' so that contemplative doctrine 'signet et determinet' operative practice; axioms of transformation ('praeceptum sive axioma de transformatione corporum') are to be framed with operational applicability in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish scope of knowledge: particular (subject-limited) vs true/formal knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge that locates a cause only 'in certis tantum subjectis' is imperfect; true knowledge that identifies the form/law embraces unity across materials and fixes the limits of nature comprehensively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon contrasts artisan-knowledge (effective on specific materials) with scientific knowledge of forms which 'complectitur in materiis dissimillimis' and allows discovery of effects not otherwise produced by industry, chance, or mere thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse forms into simpler 'clauses' or 'simple natures' for investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms (formes copulatae) should be resolvable into component 'clauses' or 'simple natures' so that investigation can proceed by examining constituent differentiae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon refers to 'paragraphos' (clauses) and the breaking down of composite forms (e.g., lion, gold) into 'conjugium naturarum simplicium' facilitating analytic induction (see Aph. 17 and related notes).
